label: Descriptive versus reference-fixed naming of GOD_4 under the necessary-being box
summary: Owner-queued slice (step 2 of 5, refs #1784): Kripke-style naming senses at the God-existence stage, connecting the idle rigid-designation library (MODAL-RIGID-DESIGNATION) to the root route. Analyst formulations, attribution deferred; Naming and Necessity was not read or cited (its source-search attempt stays blocked). Findings. (1) The stage-one naming premises (reduced e39a4fce, fuller 1ec205ed, MaximeEnsIsGod 957a71fe) are non-modal: they evaluate the name in one model, and at the reference world the descriptive (GOD_NAMING_1) and reference-fixed (GOD_NAMING_2) senses designate the same bearers (Laws clause 2), so these premises are neutral between the readings; no sense choice is hidden in them. (2) The readings diverge only under a box. The box K node (cdf897a8) applies the world-invariant GOD_4 predicate to one fixed root and boxes its existence; it is logically equivalent to its GOD_NAMING_2 reading (rigidIffBoxK, through TruthCore.Results.Modal.RigidDesignation.laws). So the route already says 'God exists necessarily' in the rigid-name sense: the actual God exists at every accessible world. The route's 1ec205ed is used only at the selected world, which is exactly reference fixing. (3) The GOD_NAMING_1 reading (necessarily, something existing uniquely meets the divine description) is a different proposition: neither it nor the box node entails the other (two-world separations). It gives the box node with the open bridge NoOtherPossibleGod (only the actual GOD_4 could meet the description at an accessible world); the box node gives it with GodhoodEssentialToGod and NoOtherPossibleGod; a joint model satisfies all four. (4) Necessity of identity (question 2): for reference-fixed names with one actual bearer, co-designation persists to every accessible world where the bearer exists, and strict necessary co-designation is equivalent to necessary existence; for descriptive names actual co-designation need not persist even when the bearer exists (control). The route's identities (first mover = maximum, De ente source = GOD_4 root) are de re equalities of Lean terms, so they need no Kripke principle; the principle concerns names and never supplies the necessary existence the box node asserts, which comes from the route's own 25 inputs. (5) Rival assessment under the substantive-objection standard: no route step uses a world-relative attribute claim (GOD_4 and the classical attributes are world-invariant predicates applied at w), so the Kripke point that a reference-fixing description need not hold of its bearer at other worlds yields no substantive objection to any existing route step; it marks what the route does not claim (that the root meets the divine description or has the attributes at other worlds). The descriptive reading's two bridges are open; positive support in the classical framework is the identity of God with his deity and the incommunicability of the divine nature (ST I q.3 a.3, q.11 a.3; supports, not attributed or formalized here). The separating models are formal interpretations only, not evidence against either bridge. Rejected readings: a third Lean sense for 'a name whose sense is the description' (it has the world-intension of GOD_NAMING_1 under narrow scope and of GOD_NAMING_2 under wide scope; the remaining difference, what is knowable a priori, is not modal-semantic); registering rigid-to-box as a strength order (the two are equivalent; recorded with logically_equivalent_to plus a sense-bridge argument that adds no warrant).
blocker: GodAt is a primitive world-indexed predicate; the route's description vocabulary (InAct, MoreIn, CausesIn, ComponentOf) is world-invariant, so the bridges NoOtherPossibleGod and GodhoodEssentialToGod cannot yet be derived from the route's own premises. Next test: index the nominal description (NominalGod) by worlds over a shared frame and try to derive GodhoodEssentialToGod from an esse-is-essence premise and NoOtherPossibleGod from at-most-one subsistent being across accessible worlds.
